2	
3	A Rule 30 engine and two statistics scripts. Node 22, ES modules, no
4	dependencies, no build step.
5	
6	## These produce empirical evidence only
7	
8	The three [Rule 30 prize questions](https://writings.stephenwolfram.com/2019/10/announcing-the-rule-30-prizes/)
9	are open. Nothing in this directory bears on whether they are true.
10	
11	- **Aperiodicity.** `periodscan.mjs` can only rule out the periods it tests, up
12	  to the number of terms it has. Finding no period below some bound is not
13	  evidence of aperiodicity — it is the absence of one particular kind of
14	  evidence for periodicity. And no amount of computation will change that:
15	  the configuration is an infinite row growing by two cells per step, so there
16	  is no finite state space to exhaust, and therefore no *N* past which a null
17	  result becomes conclusive.
18	- **Balance.** `centercolumn.mjs` reports a density near 0.5. A statement about
19	  an asymptotic limit is not testable by any finite prefix. A sequence can sit
20	  at 0.5 for a billion terms and converge to 0.4.
21	- **Irreducibility.** Nothing here addresses it at all. It is a claim about
22	  lower bounds on computation, and running a program fast says nothing about
23	  what a cleverer program could not do.
24	
25	What the explorer is actually for: sanity-checking the Lean definitions against
26	a fast independent implementation, and making the sequence concrete enough to
27	have intuitions about. Treat every number it prints as a description of a
28	finite prefix.
29	
30	## Scripts
31	
32	| File | What it is |
33	|---|---|
34	| `rule30.mjs` | the engine — module, not a CLI |
35	| `verify.mjs` | self-check; exits non-zero on failure |
36	| `centercolumn.mjs` | center column + running density of 1s (prize question 2) |
37	| `periodscan.mjs` | search for eventual periodicity (prize question 1) |
38	| `spinecheck.mjs` | engine check of the inversion identity behind the adjacent-columns theorem (prize question 1) |
39	
40	### verify.mjs
41	
42	```
43	node explorer/verify.mjs          # or: npm run verify:explorer
44	```
45	
46	Ten checks. The two that matter:
47	
48	- the BigInt engine agrees with a naive per-cell implementation over 600
49	  generations — not only on the center column but on **every cell of every
50	  row**;
51	- the first 41 center terms are the [OEIS A051023](https://oeis.org/A051023)
52	  prefix.
53	
54	The naive side is driven by the *rule number*, not by Rule 30's closed form, so
55	the two implementations share no reasoning. It also checks rule 90 against
56	binomial coefficients mod 2 and rule 254 against its light cone, which tests the
57	rule-number decoding on rules that have nothing to do with rule 30.
58	
59	One more is worth naming: a **positive control for the period scan**. A scanner
60	that reported "nothing found" regardless of its input would look exactly like a
61	correct null result on Rule 30, so `scanPeriods` is also run on a period-5
62	sequence and on one that turns periodic at index 20 — it has to find both, and
63	its onset bound has to land at or below the true onset.
64	
65	This is a check of the implementation. It is not evidence about the prize
66	questions, and the script says so when it passes.
67	
68	### centercolumn.mjs
69	
70	```
71	node explorer/centercolumn.mjs 1000000
72	npm run explore:center -- 1000000 --checkpoints=20
73	```
74	
75	| Option | |
76	|---|---|
77	| `N` | generations, default 100000 |
78	| `--checkpoints=K` | K extra evenly spaced density reports |
79	| `--no-trim` | keep every cell; slower, identical output |
80	| `--print=K` | print the first K terms |
81	| `--out=FILE` | write the column to FILE as one line of digits |
82	| `--quiet` | final line only |
83	
84	Density is reported at 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, ... up to *N*. Decade spacing is
85	deliberate: drift in a density is a question about orders of magnitude, and one
86	final number would hide it. Measured excess of 1s over 0s at a few sizes:
87	
88	| N | ones − zeros | density |
89	|---|---|---|
90	| 10,000 | +64 | 0.503200 |
91	| 100,000 | +196 | 0.500980 |
92	| 1,000,000 | +1,536 | 0.500768 |
93	| 2,000,000 | +1,418 | 0.500354 |
94	
95	The excess grows while the density shrinks, which is what a fair coin would also
96	do — the excess of a random walk grows like √N. That is a remark about what the
97	numbers look like, not a result.
98	
99	### periodscan.mjs
100	
101	```
102	node explorer/periodscan.mjs 200000
103	npm run explore:period -- 200000 --max-period=50000
104	```
105	
106	| Option | |
107	|---|---|
108	| `N` | terms of the center column, default 200000 |
109	| `--max-period=P` | largest period tested, default floor(N/2) |
110	| `--top=K` | show the K best candidates, default 10 |
111	| `--no-trim` | keep every cell; slower, identical output |
112	
113	For each period *p* it walks backwards from the last term while `s[i] === s[i-p]`
114	and records where that first fails. That failure is the **last** disagreement at
115	lag *p*, so it puts a lower bound on how late an eventual period *p* could have
116	started. Because the walk terminates almost immediately on a sequence that does
117	not repeat itself, the whole scan is about O(*P*) rather than O(*N·P*) — the
118	200,000-term scan above makes about 200,000 comparisons in total, and the time
119	is entirely in generating the sequence.
120	
121	`p > N/2` is capped away, because a period needs room to repeat at least once
122	before there is anything to observe. The output states the bound checked and
123	says explicitly what a null result does not mean.
124	
125	Candidates are ranked by **repeats** = tail length / *p*. A real period would
126	show a value far above 1. At *N* = 200,000 the best is 0.33 — the period never
127	completed even once.
128	
129	## The engine
130	
131	The whole step is one line, applied to an entire row at once:
132	
133	```js
134	next = (x << 1n) ^ (x | (x >> 1n))
135	```
136	
137	A row is a BigInt, bit *i* is cell *i*, and cell indices increase to the right.
138	The shift directions are the one genuinely confusing part:
139	
140	- bit *i* of `x << 1n` is bit *i−1* of `x`, and cell *i−1* is cell *i*'s **left**
141	  neighbour — so `x << 1n` is the left-neighbour plane, already aligned;
142	- bit *i* of `x >> 1n` is bit *i+1*, the **right** neighbour.
143	
144	Read it as: shifting *up* moves each cell's contents into a higher index, so what
145	arrives at index *i* is what used to sit at *i−1*, on the left. The shift
146	direction is the opposite of the direction the data appears to move when you draw
147	the row with low indices on the left. This is easy to get backwards; `verify.mjs`
148	is what catches it if you do.
149	
150	Two optimizations are in `centerColumn` and documented at the function:
151	
152	- **Sliding window.** The row keeps only ~512 spare zero bits below the pattern
153	  and is shifted up when the pattern eats through them, rather than reserving
154	  *N* bits of headroom up front. Every bitwise operation costs time proportional
155	  to the whole BigInt, dead zero bits included, so carrying *N* of them for *N*
156	  steps is most of the run.
157	- **Light cone (`trim`).** Information moves one cell per step, so a cell more
158	  than *N−1−g* from the center at generation *g* cannot reach the center before
159	  the run ends. Past halfway, the row is masked to that shrinking cone.
160	
161	Together these took 800,000 generations from 58s to 8.3s. `verify.mjs` checks
162	that trimming changes no term, and `--no-trim` is available on both CLIs.
163	
164	## Measured performance
165	
166	Node v22.20.0, Windows 11, one core. Wall clock for `centerColumn`, measured,
167	not extrapolated:
168	
169	| N | time |
170	|---|---|
171	| 100,000 | 0.14s |
172	| 200,000 | 0.53s |
173	| 400,000 | 2.1s |
174	| 800,000 | 8.3s |
175	| 1,000,000 | 12.8s |
176	| 1,400,000 | 75s |
177	| 2,000,000 | 207s |
178	
179	Up to about a million generations this tracks the expected quadratic curve
180	closely: the row is ~2*g* bits wide at generation *g*, so the total bit-work is
181	inherently O(*N²*) however tight the inner loop is. There is no arrangement of
182	BigInt operations that avoids that.
183	
184	Past a million it degrades faster than quadratic — 1M → 1.4M costs 5.9× where
185	quadratic predicts 2.0×. Raising the young-generation size (`--max-semi-space-size=64`)
186	did not help, so it is not simply nursery GC; beyond that the cause is
187	undiagnosed and the numbers above are reported as measured rather than
188	explained. Peak RSS stayed under 100 MB throughout.
189	
190	**Practical ceiling: about 1,000,000 generations in ~13s, and 2,000,000 if you
191	are willing to wait three and a half minutes.** Anything larger has not been
192	measured here, and the curve above is a reason not to guess.

### periodscan.mjs

```
node explorer/periodscan.mjs 200000
npm run explore:period -- 200000 --max-period=50000
```

| Option | |
|---|---|
| `N` | terms of the center column, default 200000 |
| `--max-period=P` | largest period tested, default floor(N/2) |
| `--top=K` | show the K best candidates, default 10 |
| `--no-trim` | keep every cell; slower, identical output |

For each period *p* it walks backwards from the last term while `s[i] === s[i-p]`
and records where that first fails. That failure is the **last** disagreement at
lag *p*, so it puts a lower bound on how late an eventual period *p* could have
started. Because the walk terminates almost immediately on a sequence that does
not repeat itself, the whole scan is about O(*P*) rather than O(*N·P*) — the
200,000-term scan above makes about 200,000 comparisons in total, and the time
is entirely in generating the sequence.

`p > N/2` is capped away, because a period needs room to repeat at least once
before there is anything to observe. The output states the bound checked and
says explicitly what a null result does not mean.

Candidates are ranked by **repeats** = tail length / *p*. A real period would
show a value far above 1. At *N* = 200,000 the best is 0.33 — the period never
completed even once.

## The engine

The whole step is one line, applied to an entire row at once:

```js
next = (x << 1n) ^ (x | (x >> 1n))
```

A row is a BigInt, bit *i* is cell *i*, and cell indices increase to the right.
The shift directions are the one genuinely confusing part:

- bit *i* of `x << 1n` is bit *i−1* of `x`, and cell *i−1* is cell *i*'s **left**
  neighbour — so `x << 1n` is the left-neighbour plane, already aligned;
- bit *i* of `x >> 1n` is bit *i+1*, the **right** neighbour.

Read it as: shifting *up* moves each cell's contents into a higher index, so what
arrives at index *i* is what used to sit at *i−1*, on the left. The shift
direction is the opposite of the direction the data appears to move when you draw
the row with low indices on the left. This is easy to get backwards; `verify.mjs`
is what catches it if you do.

Two optimizations are in `centerColumn` and documented at the function:

- **Sliding window.** The row keeps only ~512 spare zero bits below the pattern
  and is shifted up when the pattern eats through them, rather than reserving
  *N* bits of headroom up front. Every bitwise operation costs time proportional
  to the whole BigInt, dead zero bits included, so carrying *N* of them for *N*
  steps is most of the run.
- **Light cone (`trim`).** Information moves one cell per step, so a cell more
  than *N−1−g* from the center at generation *g* cannot reach the center before
  the run ends. Past halfway, the row is masked to that shrinking cone.

Together these took 800,000 generations from 58s to 8.3s. `verify.mjs` checks
that trimming changes no term, and `--no-trim` is available on both CLIs.

## Measured performance

Node v22.20.0, Windows 11, one core. Wall clock for `centerColumn`, measured,
not extrapolated:

| N | time |
|---|---|
| 100,000 | 0.14s |
| 200,000 | 0.53s |
| 400,000 | 2.1s |
| 800,000 | 8.3s |
| 1,000,000 | 12.8s |
| 1,400,000 | 75s |
| 2,000,000 | 207s |

Up to about a million generations this tracks the expected quadratic curve
closely: the row is ~2*g* bits wide at generation *g*, so the total bit-work is
inherently O(*N²*) however tight the inner loop is. There is no arrangement of
BigInt operations that avoids that.

Past a million it degrades faster than quadratic — 1M → 1.4M costs 5.9× where
quadratic predicts 2.0×. Raising the young-generation size (`--max-semi-space-size=64`)
did not help, so it is not simply nursery GC; beyond that the cause is
undiagnosed and the numbers above are reported as measured rather than
explained. Peak RSS stayed under 100 MB throughout.

**Practical ceiling: about 1,000,000 generations in ~13s, and 2,000,000 if you
are willing to wait three and a half minutes.** Anything larger has not been
measured here, and the curve above is a reason not to guess.

## 1. The residual, in one paragraph

Picture the rule 30 triangle with time running down. The centre column is
the vertical line through the apex. The wall asks: if that column ever
settles into a repeating pattern, show that some *other* vertical line
repeats too. Nothing else is needed, because Jen's theorem
(`isEventuallyPeriodic_column_unique`, on the board) already says two
distinct repeating columns are impossible, so the two facts together would
say the centre column never repeats, which is the first prize conjecture.
Since a contradiction implies anything, the residual is *exactly* the prize:
it is enough to show that a repeating centre column forces something false.
The residual lives on the seam between the two halves of the picture: the
right half, whose diagonals are all periodic from their first cell, and the
left half, whose diagonals settle from the edge inward and whose settled
part never reaches column zero.

## 2. Why the known routes fail

- **The diagonal structure never reaches the centre column**
  (`docs/obstructions.md`). Both the left and the right diagonal through
  the cell `(t, 0)` start there: the centre cell is index 0 of
  `leftDiagonal t` and of `rightDiagonal t`. Periodicity of a diagonal is
  a statement about indices past its onset; index 0 is never past it for
  the right family in any useful sense (period `2^t` at index 0 says
  nothing) and is inside the transient for the left family. Confirmed
  again by the scan below: right diagonal `k` has minimal period
  `2^m(k)` with `m(k)` growing with `k`, so the period at the centre
  cell's own diagonal is unbounded.
- **Two adjacent columns propagate left** (`evolve_period_sub`,
  `not_evolve_period_adjacent`, Kopra 2022 Thm 3.5). This is why the
  width-2 case closes: a shared period in columns 0 and 1 walks left by
  the sideways inverse and hits the black left edge. With one column the
  sideways inverse has a free input at every time the centre is black
  (see claim C2), so nothing propagates. This is not a new dead end, it is
  the gap the wall names.
- **New dead end, recorded below in `docs/obstructions.md` as "The centre
  column as a boundary condition".** The right half-line `x ≥ 1` and the
  left half-line `x ≤ -1` are each driven by column 0 alone as their only
  boundary, with an all-white start. So one is tempted to prove the
  residual as a statement about a half-line automaton with a periodic
  boundary sequence, forgetting where the sequence came from. That
  statement is false: the constant boundary `c ≡ true` makes columns 1
  and 2 of the right half-line constant from row 2 on. Any proof must use
  that `c` is the centre column of the *single seed*, which is the same
  as using the white cone on the left. Details in C1.
